Reputational Risk Management: How Companies Map, Score and Control Reputation Risks

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Reputational risk management is the discipline of identifying where damage to a company's reputation could come from, estimating how likely and how serious each scenario is, and putting controls and owners in place before anything happens. For most Italian companies it does not require a new department, but a short risk register, a scoring method and clear responsibilities shared between management, communications, legal and HR.

Reputation is a consequence of other risks

Reputational risk rarely appears on its own: it is the public, amplified consequence of an operational, legal, ethical or commercial failure. A delayed delivery becomes a wave of one-star reviews, a dismissal becomes a viral post, a supplier's labour violation becomes a headline about your brand.

This is why treating reputation as a communications problem alone fails. The useful question for a board in Milan or a family business in Veneto is not "how do we respond?" but "which of our processes could produce a story we would not want to read online, and how visible would it be?" Online platforms have shortened the distance between an internal problem and public exposure to hours, which makes web reputation risks the part of the map that needs the closest attention.

Mapping where reputational risk comes from

A complete map starts from stakeholders, because every damaging story has a source and a channel. Listing them systematically prevents the common bias of focusing only on customer reviews.

SourceTypical triggerWhere it surfaces online
CustomersService failures, billing disputes, product defectsGoogle reviews, marketplaces, social media, consumer forums
Employees and former staffDismissals, workplace conflicts, safety incidentsEmployer review sites, LinkedIn, anonymous posts, union statements
Partners and shareholdersContract disputes, exits, litigationPress, court rulings, sector blogs
Supply chainLabour or environmental violations by suppliersNGO reports, investigative journalism
Regulators and authoritiesFines, inspections, AGCM or Garante decisionsOfficial publications, news agencies, search results for the brand
ManagementPersonal conduct, statements, past news about executivesSearch results for executives' names, social media

For each source, write down concrete scenarios rather than abstract categories. "A former sales manager publishes a detailed post accusing the company of unpaid bonuses" can be assessed and prevented; "employee dissatisfaction" cannot.

Scoring likelihood and impact

Each scenario gets two scores, usually on a scale from one to five: how likely it is within the next year, and how much harm it would cause if it happened. Multiplying them produces a priority ranking that management can actually discuss.

  1. Likelihood – based on past incidents, sector patterns and the current state of controls; a company with recurring delivery complaints scores high on review-driven scenarios.
  2. Impact – assessed across several dimensions: lost revenue, effect on hiring, financing and partner relationships, regulatory consequences and the persistence of content in search results.
  3. Velocity – how quickly the damage would spread; a social media incident can peak in a day, while a court ruling surfaces slowly but stays for years.
  4. Visibility – whether the content would appear on page one for the brand name, which multiplies the effective impact of almost any event.

Scores should be reviewed by people from different functions, because sales, HR and legal see different signals. The way reputation translates into valuation and access to capital, which should inform the impact score, is analysed in our article on how online reputation affects company value.

Prevention controls that reduce the score

Controls are what turn a risk register into protection: each high-priority scenario should have at least one measure that lowers its likelihood and one that limits its impact. Many of them are inexpensive and already partly present in Italian companies.

  • A documented protocol for responding to reviews and complaints within a defined time, with escalation to management for serious cases.
  • A social media policy for employees and a respectful exit process, which reduce the risk of hostile posts by former staff.
  • Supplier due diligence and contractual clauses on labour and environmental standards, with audit rights.
  • An internal whistleblowing channel compliant with Legislative Decree 24/2023, so that problems reach management before they reach journalists.
  • Verification of marketing and sustainability claims, since misleading statements are both an AGCM risk and a reputational one.
  • Continuous monitoring of brand and executive searches, reviews and mentions, so that early signals are noticed.

Early-warning indicators deserve particular attention; our article on the signs that a reputational attack is being prepared lists the patterns that typically precede a coordinated campaign.

Who owns reputational risk

Every risk in the register needs a named owner responsible for its controls, while overall accountability sits with top management. Without ownership, reputation becomes everyone's concern and nobody's task.

In practice, the board or managing director approves the risk register and reviews it at least annually. Function heads own the scenarios arising in their areas: HR for employee-related risks, procurement for the supply chain, customer service for reviews. Communications and legal act as cross-functional owners for response. Companies that have adopted an organisational model under Legislative Decree 231/2001 can integrate reputational scenarios into the same risk assessment, since many offences covered by the model carry heavy reputational consequences.

A risk without an owner is a risk the company has decided, by default, to accept.

Measuring whether the system works

Reputation risk management works when incidents are caught earlier, handled faster and leave fewer lasting traces in search results. Those outcomes can be tracked with a small set of indicators reviewed every quarter.

Useful measures include the share of page-one results for the brand that are neutral or positive, average rating and its trend on the main review platforms, median response time to negative reviews, the number of issues detected internally before they became public, and the presence of any regulatory or legal content in branded searches. A sudden change in any of these should trigger a review of the related scenarios.
